options: A permission granted to a login to read a specific table
The size of the transaction log file
The total physical RAM installed on the server
Workspace memory that SQL Server reserves for operators like sorts and hash joins before a query begins executing
questions.explain: Certain plan operators need a memory workspace to do their job, and that workspace is reserved up front as a memory grant, sized by the optimizer's estimate.

questions.q: What does sys.dm_exec_query_memory_grants expose about a query with a NULL grant_time but a populated request_time?
options: The query has already finished executing successfully
The query's plan has been evicted from cache
The query is still waiting for its memory grant to be satisfied — the query-level view of a RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE wait
The query never requested a memory grant at all
questions.explain: A request without a grant time means the grant hasn't been satisfied yet — the session is queued, which is exactly what RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE tracks at the wait-stats level.

questions.q: Why can RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits occur even on a server with abundant physical RAM?
options: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE is unrelated to memory and always indicates a CPU problem
Abundant RAM guarantees RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits can never happen
SQL Server ignores physical RAM entirely when granting query memory
The memory available for query grants is a bounded, shared pool (not all of physical RAM), and it can be exhausted by too many concurrent large grant requests
questions.explain: The grant pool is a bounded budget separate from total physical RAM; concurrent demand exceeding that budget causes queuing regardless of how much RAM the server has overall.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the most common underlying root cause of an overestimated memory grant?
options: A bad cardinality estimate from the optimizer, often due to stale statistics or parameter sniffing
TempDB having too many data files
The server having too much physical memory installed
The transaction log being too small
questions.explain: Grant size is based on estimated row counts; when that estimate is wrong (stale stats, parameter sniffing, poorly handled correlations), the grant requested can be drastically oversized.

questions.q: A query shows granted_memory_kb of 2,000,000 and max_used_memory_kb of only 15,000. Is 'increase max server memory' the right first fix, per this lesson?
options: No — the large gap points at an overestimated grant from a bad cardinality estimate; the fix is addressing the estimate (statistics, parameter sniffing, or a rewrite), not adding server memory
Yes — increasing memory is the only way sys.dm_exec_query_memory_grants gaps can be resolved
Yes — this always means the server simply doesn't have enough RAM
No — this gap is normal and requires no investigation at all
questions.explain: A grant far larger than what was actually used is the signature of an overestimated grant from a bad row-count estimate, which server memory alone doesn't fix.
